issues.subcategory: contradictory SESOI specification within same section
issues.description: The formal analytic plan specifies an equivalence region of δ=.27, yet the rationale immediately following in the same section states the SESOI is set to δ=|.11|, explicitly calling this 'an extremely conservative analytic decision.' These two values differ by a factor of nearly 2.5 and cannot both define the pre-specified equivalence interval. For a registered report, precise pre-specification of the primary equivalence region is essential; this ambiguity allows post-hoc selection of the threshold that best fits obtained results. It is entirely unclear which value will govern the primary equivalence tests for gambling and substance analyses.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27. [...] setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence operationalized as 'severity of consequences' rather than frequency
issues.description: The entire theoretical framework defines moral incongruence as 'the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior.' However, a pivotal sentence in the present study section redefines it as 'the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.' Severity of consequences is a fundamentally different construct from frequency of use: a person may use a behavior frequently with few consequences or rarely with severe consequences. This slip likely reflects confusion between the NIDA-ASSIST frequency items and consequence items, but as written it introduces an operationalization that contradicts every other description in the paper and undermines the construct validity of the key predictor. The moderation tests described everywhere else use frequency, not consequences, so readers cannot determine what is actually being measured.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action. That is, the present study seeks to test whether the observed effects of interactions present in prior literature for pornography use (i.e., between moral disapproval and frequency of use) extend to addictive disorders more broadly.

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale description contradicts supplemental materials
issues.description: The methods section describes the PGSI as a '4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always),' matching the validated standard scoring. The supplemental materials, however, show the actual response options coded as Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). This 0/2/4/5 coding is non-standard, has unequal intervals (gaps of 2, 2, then only 1 between the last two options), and makes scores incomparable to any published PGSI norm or clinical cutoff. The anomalous '5' for 'Almost Always' (rather than 6, which would maintain equal spacing) is unexplained. Additionally, the methods state 'Responses will be averaged,' whereas the standard PGSI uses summed scores with established diagnostic cutoffs (0–1 = non-problem, 2–7 = moderate risk, 8+ = problem gambling). Both deviations render PGSI scores uninterpretable against the validation literature.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions (e.g., 'Have you felt that you might have a problem with gambling?' and 'Has gambling caused you any health problems, including stress or anxiety?') on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale description contradicts supplemental materials
issues.description: The methods section describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' with responses summed, implying a maximum total score of 10. The supplemental materials reveal the actual response coding as Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4), creating a 0/2/4 metric with a possible summed range of 0–20. This doubles the scale range relative to what is described, substantially changing score distributions and their interpretation. The non-standard coding is neither acknowledged in the methods nor referenced against the validated BPS scoring (Kraus et al., 2020). Readers and future replicators have no way to reconcile the described '0 to 2' scale with the actual '0 to 4' maximum per item.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, 'In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?' by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors (e.g., 'You have attempted to "cut back" or stop using pornography, but were unsuccessful.') on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: same effect size reported with two different Cohen's d values in same paragraph
issues.description: The effect from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020) with ΔR²=.012 and f²=.016 is first reported with Cohen's d=.22 and then, three sentences later when justifying the SESOI, reported with Cohen's d=.25 for the identical citation and identical ΔR²/f² values. These cannot both be correct. Furthermore, neither value is consistent with the standard conversion formula d ≈ 2√f², which yields d ≈ .253 for f²=.016 (closer to .25 but not .22). Similarly, the first listed effect (ΔR²=.014, f²=.020, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020) reports d=.24, but the formula yields d ≈ .283. The pattern of errors in the smaller effects—but not the larger ones (f²=.12 → d=.69 ✓; f²=.23 → d=.97 ✓)—suggests a systematic error in converting small effect sizes that undermines confidence in the SESOI rationale.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: inappropriate averaging of incompatible response scales in NIDA-ASSIST composite
issues.description: The planned NIDA-ASSIST problematic use composite averages five items using two incompatible response scales: three frequency items use a 0–5 scale (urges, health/social/legal/financial problems, role impairment), while two yes/no items use a 0/3/6 scale (friend/family concern, failure to control). Averaging across items with such different scale ranges and effective variances is statistically inappropriate. The 0/3/6 items have a range three times larger than the 0–5 items, meaning they will dominate the composite in an unintended and unquantified way. Simple averaging also ignores that the original NIDA-ASSIST uses a differential, weighted scoring algorithm. The resulting composite will have unknown psychometric properties, inflated variance from the 0/3/6 items, and no reference validity data.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis). [...] Participants will also respond to two questions... for each substance on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months).

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency scale starting point inconsistent across sections
issues.description: The methods section describes the pornography frequency scale as ranging from '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).' The supplemental materials show the actual scale anchored at Never (0) through More than Once Per Day (5)—identical to the substance use frequency scale described in the same section as '0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day).' The 1-to-6 description in the text is internally contradictory with the supplement and creates a consequential error in the exclusion criterion: 'scores > 1 on the frequency measure' means any use if the scale is 1–6 (never=1), but means monthly or more frequent use if the scale is 0–5 (never=0, once-or-twice=1). This would systematically exclude once-or-twice-per-year pornography users from all addiction analyses under the correct 0–5 scale.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). Like the above-described process for the ASSIST, only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below.

issues.subcategory: direct contradiction between conditional and unconditional measure administration
issues.description: The data screening section explicitly states that 'key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.' However, the substance use section states 'Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use,' and the pornography section states 'only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months...will complete the remaining items.' These are irreconcilably contradictory. The unconditional approach would mean non-users are asked about addiction symptoms (undermining construct validity and artificially inflating the user sample for moral incongruence tests). The conditional approach contradicts the stated design. This also affects power calculations in Table 2, which assume user-only subsamples.
issues.quote: key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample. [...] Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: sports-wagering oversample confounds gambling analyses without weighting plan
issues.description: The study combines a nationally representative sample (n=2,500) with 1,500 specifically recruited sports-wagering individuals for a total of 4,000. The power analysis treats this as a single combined gambling analysis sample (effective n=3,325). Because sports bettors are overrepresented by design (they constitute ~45% of the total n but represent far fewer than 45% of the U.S. gambling population), the combined sample is systematically non-representative for any gambling-related variable. Sports bettors may have systematically different moral attitudes toward gambling, problem gambling profiles, and gambling frequencies compared to lottery players, casino gamblers, or non-gamblers. No weighting procedure, separate analysis plan, or acknowledgment of this bias in the gambling-specific findings is provided.
issues.quote: Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency described as multi-item average but only one item exists in supplement
issues.description: The methods state 'Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.' This wording implies multiple gambling frequency items to be averaged into a composite. However, the supplemental materials contain only a single gambling frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). There is no multi-item gambling frequency battery to average across. This discrepancy between described and actual measurement leaves the gambling frequency operationalization fundamentally unclear and prevents replication.
issues.quote: Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale described above, ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: dual outcome measures for pornography and gambling without primary outcome designation
issues.description: For both pornography and gambling, two separate outcome measures are planned: a validated scale (BPS or PGSI) and the modified NIDA-ASSIST composite. The analytic plan states '8 moderation analyses...corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest' but Table 1 lists only 7 behaviors, suggesting both outcomes for pornography and/or gambling will be analyzed. No pre-specification identifies which outcome is primary for the key equivalence tests for these behaviors. Running multiple overlapping tests of the central hypothesis without a designated primary outcome permits selective emphasis on whichever result better supports the uniqueness claim for pornography. This is a significant registered-report deviation because confirmatory tests require a single pre-specified outcome.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: predetermined conclusion framing undermines confirmatory registered report design
issues.description: The paper explicitly frames its aim as 'to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior.' Framing a confirmatory study as designed to 'demonstrate' a predetermined position conflates advocacy with hypothesis testing, which is incompatible with the registered report format whose purpose is to commit to inference rules before observing data. This framing is further compounded by the asymmetric hypothesis structure: pornography is tested with a standard significance test, while gambling and substances are tested for equivalence with null—a design specifically suited to declare the null when desired. The stated aim of demonstrating uniqueness before the data are collected introduces directional bias in every decision about operationalization, SESOI selection, and interpretation.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: number of planned moderation analyses inconsistent with table of outcomes
issues.description: The analytic plan states 'we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest.' Table 1, however, lists exactly 7 target behaviors (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, pornography, gambling). No explanation reconciles the discrepancy between 8 analyses and 7 table rows. If the 8th analysis arises from running both the BPS and NIDA-ASSIST for pornography or both the PGSI and NIDA-ASSIST for gambling, the design requires 9 analyses (or 9 for pornography + gambling × 2 + 5 substances = 9). The counting error has direct implications for multiple comparison corrections and the structure of the primary confirmatory tests.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: no multiple comparison correction for primary moderation analyses
issues.description: Seven or eight moderation analyses will be conducted using OLS regression at α=.05, but no correction for multiple comparisons across these tests is pre-specified. The only mention of multiple comparison correction is Holm adjustment for bivariate correlations, which are explicitly secondary. With 7–8 correlated tests, the uncorrected familywise error rate for Type I errors is approximately 30%. Because the critical pornography hypothesis requires a significant interaction (p<.05), the absence of a familywise correction makes it easier to achieve a 'significant' pornography finding relative to the null/equivalence results for other behaviors. This asymmetry directly favors confirmation of the uniqueness hypothesis.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests using the reg.equiv.fd function (Alter & Counsell, 2021).

issues.subcategory: pervasive causal language in cross-sectional design
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, the relationship between moral incongruence and self-reported addiction is described with directional causal language: 'moral disapproval likely amplifies the links,' 'moral incongruence predicts feeling out of control,' 'moral incongruence regarding pornography use itself seems to predict greater experience of depression.' The proposed study is entirely cross-sectional, measuring all variables simultaneously at a single time point. Cross-sectional moderation analyses establish covariation patterns, not temporal precedence. The reverse pathway—feeling out of control causing moral reappraisal and increased retrospective disapproval—is equally consistent with the proposed design. While the limitation section acknowledges cross-sectional design, the causal framing permeating the introduction and hypothesis statements systematically overstates what the design can support.
issues.quote: moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction... moral incongruence regarding pornography use itself seems to predict greater experience of depression in men.

issues.subcategory: fallback equivalence region partially determined by obtained pornography results
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies that if gambling or substance moral incongruence effects exceed the primary SESOI equivalence region, 'exploratory analyses' will redefine the equivalence region 'using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.' This means the equivalence region for gambling and substance analyses depends on confidence interval values obtained from the current study's pornography analysis—values that will not be known until the data are collected. This creates a partially post-hoc equivalence interval that cannot be fully pre-specified before data collection and introduces circular reasoning (using a result from the study to define the decision criterion for other analyses within the same study). A secondary fallback region should be fixed from prior literature, not derived from the current study's results.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: critically underpowered subgroups undermine equivalence claims for key substances
issues.description: Table 2 shows that prescription drug misuse (estimated effective n=140) achieves only 30.1% power to detect the SESOI (f²=.015), and illicit drug use (n=240–480) achieves 47.2–76.4% power. These are far below the 80% threshold, rendering equivalence claims for these substances essentially uninformative. The proposed fallback—shifting to a larger equivalence region based on a prior pornography estimate—fundamentally changes the research question from 'is the effect null?' to 'is the effect smaller than the pornography effect?', which is a qualitatively weaker inference. Yet the abstract and introduction present the study as testing moral incongruence 'for a variety of behaviors' without adequately foregrounding that two substance categories are insufficiently powered for the primary equivalence claim.
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small.

issues.subcategory: unvalidated NIDA-ASSIST application to pornography and gambling
issues.description: The study adds pornography and gambling as items within the NIDA-ASSIST, a tool validated exclusively for substance use screening. The authors acknowledge 'such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography' but assert this 'will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses' without empirical justification. Applying a substance screening instrument to behavioral addictions with different reinforcement schedules, social contexts, and consequence patterns introduces unknown and unquantifiable measurement error. Because the NIDA-ASSIST pornography and gambling composites will serve as secondary outcome measures in the key moderation analyses, their unknown psychometric properties (reliability, factor structure, convergent validity) threaten validity of any conclusions drawn from them.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: no missing data plan despite certainty of at least some missingness
issues.description: The data screening section states 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data,' relying entirely on YouGov's undisclosed proprietary procedures. No plan is provided for handling missing data should it occur—no mention of listwise deletion, multiple imputation, full information maximum likelihood, or any other approach. This is unrealistic even for well-administered online surveys, particularly given the sensitive nature of questions about illegal drug use, prescription drug misuse, sexual behavior, and moral attitudes. For a registered report, pre-specifying missing data handling is standard practice because post-hoc decisions are a source of analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: primary alcohol frequency variable not designated among competing measures
issues.description: The methods include both a general alcohol frequency item ('how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed') and sex-specific heavy episodic drinking items (>4 drinks/occasion for women; >5 drinks/occasion for men). The general frequency item is described as the one 'we will look at for the present study,' but both measures will be collected and the heavy drinking items are explicitly retained. No pre-specification clarifies whether general frequency or heavy episodic drinking frequency will serve as the predictor in the moral incongruence moderation analysis for alcohol. These capture distinct constructs (any drinking vs. risky drinking) with different expected relationships to moral disapproval and problem outcomes, and the choice will meaningfully affect results.
issues.quote: In its original form, the NIDA Quick Screen asks men to report alcohol frequency in terms of how many days they have consumed five or more drinks in a day and women to report alcohol frequency in terms of days they have consumed four or more drinks per day. Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: binary gender operationalization excludes non-binary participants and may reflect measurement mismatch
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies 'gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male)' as a covariate. YouGov panel data likely includes participants identifying with genders beyond the binary. Collapsing all non-male gender identities into a single category loses information about potentially meaningful variation in moral disapproval and addiction patterns across gender groups. Furthermore, the 'not-male' coding implicitly treats all non-male identities as equivalent, which is both conceptually problematic and inconsistent with standard practices in survey research. No justification for the binary coding is provided, and no sensitivity analysis is planned for participants excluded or conflated by this coding.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.subcategory: centering procedure not fully specified for moderation analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated,' but does not specify whether centering means mean-centering or standardization (z-scoring). More critically, it does not specify the centering reference group: the full sample (including non-users with frequency=0) or the user subsample. For behaviors with substantial proportions of non-users (e.g., illicit drugs, prescription drug misuse), centering on the full sample vs. the user subsample will produce different interaction terms with different magnitudes and interpretations, affecting both the main effects and the critical interaction estimates.
issues.quote: Additionally, focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated. Key dependent variables are listed in Table 1.

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measure with unknown reliability as key moderator
issues.description: Moral disapproval—the critical moderator in every planned interaction test—is assessed with a single item per behavior. Single-item measures cannot have internal reliability estimated, have limited content validity by definition, and contain random measurement error that attenuates regression coefficients and particularly interaction terms. Attenuation of the moral disapproval × frequency interaction for gambling and substances (due to measurement error) would spuriously support the authors' hypothesis that these interactions fall within the equivalence region. Conversely, attenuation of the pornography interaction would work against their hypothesis. The planned reliability analyses (Cronbach's alpha and Omega total) explicitly cannot be applied to single-item measures, yet are listed as part of the analytic plan.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). [...] Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach's alpha and Omega total), will be calculated.

issues.subcategory: religiousness included as covariate may suppress key moral disapproval effects
issues.description: Religiousness is included as a covariate in all moderation models. However, religiousness is described throughout the introduction as one of the primary antecedents and correlates of moral disapproval of pornography (the two variables are highly correlated). Including a covariate that substantially shares variance with the key predictor (moral disapproval) and moderator in the interaction will suppress both the main effect of moral disapproval and the moral incongruence interaction through multicollinearity. This could deflate the pornography interaction, potentially failing to support the study's primary hypothesis, while also deflating gambling and substance interactions, potentially supporting the equivalence hypothesis for those behaviors. The decision to control for religiousness rather than model it as a mediator or separate moderator is underspecified and could systematically bias results in either direction.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates, as prior work has demonstrated clear links between such variables and self-reported problematic pornography use.
